# dump978-fa

**Decoder for 978 MHz UAT, the second ADS-B link -- US general aviation below 18,000 ft**

- **Version recorded:** 11.1
- **Categories:** `aircraft`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/flightaware/dump978>

## What it does

dump978-fa decodes UAT, the ADS-B link on 978 MHz, from an SDR through SoapySDR. It listens on the frequency, demodulates the bursts, corrects their errors and serves what it hears: raw messages on a TCP port (`--raw-port`, 30978 by FlightAware's convention), decoded JSON on another (`--json-port`), or either on standard output. The second program, `skyaware978`, connects to that raw port and keeps an `aircraft.json` and its history up to date in a directory, the files a web map reads. Receive only.

## Why you would want it

In the United States, aircraft flying below 18,000 feet may carry UAT instead of the 1090 MHz transponder link, and many light aircraft do. `readsb` (in this profile) hears 1090 MHz only, so without this a US receiver misses those aircraft; UAT also carries the FIS-B weather and TIS-B traffic the ground stations broadcast. Outside the US there is usually nothing on 978 MHz to hear. readsb can take dump978-fa's raw port as a second input (`--net-connector 127.0.0.1,30978,uat_in`) and show both links in one set of JSON.

## Before it will work

An SDR that tunes 978 MHz -- an RTL-SDR is the usual one -- with an antenna cut for 978 MHz, and the SoapySDR module for that receiver: `soapysdr-module-rtlsdr` for an RTL-SDR (the `rtl-sdr` hardware entry lists it). FlightAware's package starts it as `dump978-fa --sdr driver=rtlsdr --format CS8 --raw-port 30978 --json-port 30979` (`debian/dump978-fa.default` in the tree); run by hand, write the ports as `127.0.0.1:30978` and `127.0.0.1:30979` unless you mean other machines to reach them.

## Known problems

**It needs its own receiver.** A dongle on 978 MHz cannot also be listening on 1090 MHz, so UAT and 1090 together means two dongles, and any program already holding the device stops it starting. **A port given without a host listens on every interface**: `--raw-port 30978` serves what your receiver hears to the whole network, so name 127.0.0.1 unless that is the intent. Nothing in this build starts at boot: FlightAware's package adds a systemd service, an account and a lighttpd page (SkyAware978), and this manifest installs only the two programs. The web page itself is not installed.
What was measured: built on Debian 13 and Kali; both programs print their help (`--help`, exit status 64). Upstream's own sample of 1,143 raw UAT messages (439 from aircraft, the rest ground uplinks), stamped with the current time and served on a loopback port in dump978-fa's raw format, was decoded by skyaware978 into an `aircraft.json` of 21 aircraft; skyaware978 discards messages more than 15 seconds old, so the unstamped sample decodes to nothing. With `--raw-port 30978 --json-port 127.0.0.1:30979` the container's /proc/net/tcp showed 0.0.0.0:30978 and 127.0.0.1:30979. The same sample, fed to Debian's readsb with `--net-connector 127.0.0.1,30978,uat_in`, came out in readsb's JSON as the same 21 aircraft. Not measured: an SDR, a live 978 MHz signal, FIS-B uplink decoding, or SkyAware978's web page, which is not installed.

## Keeping it current

- probe: github tags (`flightaware/dump978`)
- strategy: rebuild
- FlightAware tags with each PiAware release (v10.0 2025-02 to v11.1 2026-07). Move the tag and its commit together. The Makefile builds with -Werror, so a newer compiler or Boost can turn a warning into a failed build: rebuild on the newest target before moving.
